lead: Styling hair upward, as in a quiff or pompadour, is discussed in looksmaxxing circles as a way to add apparent height and a longer head-to-body line. A quiff has longer hair at the front combed up and back, with shorter sides, so the extra volume above the forehead raises the top of the silhouette by a few centimetres and frames the face.[1][2]

The quiff combines elements of the 1950s pompadour and flattop and was a staple of the British Teddy Boy movement, returning in the 1980s and 1990s.[2] The pompadour, a large volume of hair swept up from the forehead, was popularised in the 1950s by Elvis Presley and James Dean.[3] Adding height to hair has a longer history, beginning at the French court in the 1680s.[3]

Practitioners use blow drying, pomades, clays and overnight techniques to create volume, and forum discussion centres on how to keep fine or straight hair voluminous through the day.[4][5] No studies were found on whether upswept hair changes perceived height.

angle.text: A quiff or pompadour adds volume above the forehead, which raises the highest point of the head by a few centimetres while worn. Users also say the lifted front lengthens the face and head line.

paras: The modern quiff leaves hair longer at the front tapering toward trimmed sides and back.[2] Wikipedia describes it as a combination of the 1950s pompadour and flattop, and sometimes a mohawk, and as a post-war reaction to short, strict haircuts for men.[2] The pompadour is a large volume of hair swept upward from the forehead, sometimes upswept at the sides and back too.[3]
The Japanese Regent is a similar style, associated with yakuza and bosozoku biker gangs.[2][3] In psychobilly circles a modified pompadour is called a quiff.[3]

The origin of the word quiff is uncertain. Proposals include French coiffe (a hairstyle, or the mail coif worn under knights' helmets), Dutch kuif meaning crest, and a link to Tintin's Dutch name Kuifje, the diminutive of kuif; Tintin is depicted with a quiff.[2][1]

Height at the crown first appeared in French court hairstyles of the 1680s such as the fontange, and a taller style returned under Louis XVI before the Revolution. The pompadour is named for Madame de Pompadour, although her own style was worn back with no extra height, and the name was coined in the twentieth century.[3] Women's raised styles returned in the 1890s Gibson Girl era, again in the 1940s, and in a minor early-2000s revival created by backcombing at the roots.[3]

The men's quiff emerged in post-war Britain as a reaction to short military cuts and spread with rock and roll.[1][2] The men's pompadour rose in the 1950s with Elvis Presley and James Dean, held with pomade and Brylcreem, and the related ducktail followed; it was revived in the 1980s rockabilly scene and again in the mid-2000s.[3] Latino communities in the United States adopted the style from the 1930s to the 1960s, and it remains associated with Italian American subcultures.[3] The quiff returned to popularity in Europe in the early 1980s and again in the 1990s.[2] Wikipedia says the modern pompadour has been a trend since 2011, with television host Conan O'Brien cited as a well-known wearer.[3]

The Teddy Boy subculture, which began among teenagers in London in the early 1950s, made the greased quiff at the front with the sides combed back into a duck's-arse rear its signature hair; a Daily Express article on 23 September 1953 popularised the name, and a variant called the Boston was greased straight back and cut square at the nape [8]. In the 1970s Teds wore flamboyant pompadours with hairspray added to their grease or pomade, and revivals followed through the 1972 London Rock and Roll Show at Wembley and the 1973 films American Graffiti and That'll Be the Day [8].

Hair-cream brands shaped the mid-century look. Brylcreem, an emulsion of water and mineral oil stabilised with beeswax and known for its high shine, was first made in 1928 by County Chemicals in Birmingham, England, and its television advertising featured a cartoon man whose hair combed itself after a dab of product [9]. It later passed through Beecham, Sara Lee and, in 2012, Unilever [9].

Pomade, clay and wax products hold the shape of a quiff, and blow drying with the hair directed upward builds volume at the roots.[1] For fine or thin hair, forum users describe adding volume without product, such as tying long hair up while wet and sleeping that way, which they say leaves hair more voluminous and slightly wavy.[4]

A dermatology review on hair fullness describes medical and cosmetic approaches to increasing the apparent thickness of scalp hair, which include cosmetic styling and products.[6] A review of what constitutes healthy hair describes the properties that influence how hair looks and behaves.[7]

Hold and finish differ by product family: the high-shine creams and pomades associated with the 1950s style contrast with matte clays and waxes, and blow drying upward at the roots builds lift before product is applied [9][1]. Forum users with fine hair focus on lift at the roots and on keeping volume through the day, whereas users with thick hair focus on controlling it [4][5].

sections.h: How it affects apparent height and proportions
paras: Proponents describe the quiff as raising the top of the head line by a few centimetres while worn and lengthening the face and head relative to the body, which in looksmaxxing vocabulary relates to height and facial proportion [1][4]. The hair also frames the forehead and can balance a long or short face according to how much volume sits at the front; these are users' descriptions rather than measured results. No published study has measured whether upswept hair changes how tall a person is judged to be.

Users on looksmax.org share methods to boost volume in thin or straight hair, such as the overnight technique above.[4] Responders in the same thread report that such methods work for them while others question the reasoning.[4] Another thread asks how to keep volume from going flat after leaving the house or the gym, a common complaint among users with fine hair.[5]
No studies found on whether upswept hair changes perceived height. Related dermatology research addresses scalp hair fullness in general.[6][7]

American Graffiti and That'll Be the Day help revive 1950s styles, including pompadours [8].

Modern pompadour trend begins per Wikipedia.[3]

lore.intro: Hair volume is discussed on forums mainly as a styling challenge for fine hair, sometimes tied to looking taller.[4][5]

claims.claim: Tying hair up overnight gives 'volume' without product.
claims.believers: A looksmax.org poster says tying hair up while wet and sleeping that way leaves hair more voluminous and slightly wavy, and found it most useful for thin straight hair.[4]
claims.experts: No published studies have tested this technique.

claims.claim: Upswept hair makes you look taller.
claims.believers: Proponents say added height on top lengthens the silhouette.[4]
claims.experts: No published studies have examined hair height and perceived stature.

claims.claim: Volume fades by midday and is hard to maintain.
claims.believers: A poster describes hair that looks voluminous in the morning but goes flat after leaving school or the gym.[5]
claims.experts: Dermatology reviews describe hair fullness approaches in general terms but do not address styling longevity.[6]

claims.claim: A quiff or pompadour balances face proportions
claims.believers: Users describe volume at the front as lengthening or reframing the face and head line [4].
claims.experts: No published studies have tested this; related dermatology reviews address scalp hair fullness in general [6][7].

name: Hair volume / quiff for height

card.summary: Swept-up hair like a quiff, claimed to add height; forum talk is mostly about keeping fine hair fluffy.
card.note: No studies on hair height and perceived stature.

quick.overview:
Styling hair upward, as in a quiff or pompadour, is said by proponents to add height and a longer line.

The quiff is a 1950s-era style that has returned several times.
quick.mechanism: Hair is lifted at the front using products, blow drying or overnight techniques.
quick.risks: Low risk; styling products and heat can affect hair condition. No studies on perceived height effects were found.
